title: Don't Build Agents, Build Skills Instead – Barry Zhang & Mahesh Murag, Anthropic

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk is fundamentally about agent architecture and how to equip agents for real-world work. It introduces the converging agent architecture stack (agent loop, runtime, MCP servers, skills library), presents skills as an architectural component, and uses a computing stack analogy (models=processors, runtime=OS, skills=apps) to frame the architecture. The central thesis 'stop building agents, build skills instead' is an architectural recommendation about how to structure agent systems.

secondary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations
secondary.rationale: Skills are a new form factor for packaging tools and procedural knowledge. The talk extensively discusses how skills complement MCP servers (MCP for connectivity, skills for expertise), how scripts within skills serve as tools, and how skills solve traditional tool limitations like ambiguous instructions and context window bloat.

secondary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
secondary.rationale: Progressive disclosure is a core context window management technique that protects context while enabling hundreds of composable skills. The talk discusses continuous learning through skills, a collective knowledge base, and making memory tangible for agents—key context engineering and memory concepts.

secondary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
secondary.rationale: Skills are positioned as a developer platform with an emerging ecosystem (foundational, third-party, enterprise categories). The talk describes future directions treating skills like software (versioning, dependency management, testing) and a shared distribution model for organizational knowledge.

domains.label: Agent Systems
domains.rationale: The entire talk is about agent systems: agent architecture, agent skills, agent runtime, and the emerging agent stack combining loop, runtime, MCP, and skills.

domains.label: Developer Tooling
domains.rationale: Skills are developer tools for extending agent capabilities. The talk describes the skills ecosystem, skill creator tool, and future directions like versioning and dependency management that mirror software development tooling.

domains.label: Knowledge Management
domains.rationale: Skills package procedural knowledge and domain expertise. The talk envisions a collective, evolving knowledge base curated by people and agents, and continuous learning where agents create and share skills.

domains.label: Enterprise Ai
domains.rationale: The talk describes Fortune 100 companies and large developer productivity teams building enterprise skills, and Anthropic launching vertical-specific offerings for financial services and life sciences.

summary: Barry Zhang and Mahesh Murag of Anthropic present Agent Skills at the AI Engineering Code Summit. Their thesis: agents have intelligence but lack domain expertise, and Agent Skills — organized folders of files packaging composable procedural knowledge, including scripts as tools — bridge this gap. Skills use progressive disclosure (showing only metadata at runtime, loading full SKILL.md only when needed) to protect context windows and enable hundreds of composable capabilities. Since the October 2025 launch, thousands of skills emerged across foundational (Anthropic document skills), third-party (Browserbase, Notion), and enterprise (Fortune 100 companies) categories. Skills complement MCP servers: MCP provides external connectivity, skills provide domain expertise. The converging agent architecture combines an agent loop, runtime environment (file system + code execution), MCP servers, and a skills library. Future directions include treating skills like software — testing, versioning, dependency management — and enabling continuous learning where Claude creates skills from experience that future versions of itself can reuse. The computing analogy: models are processors, agent runtime is the OS, skills are applications. The call to action: stop rebuilding agents, start building skills. First-party Anthropic sources (engineering blog, GitHub repo, platform docs, product announcements) and secondary reporting (Business Insider) corroborate the talk's key claims. One unverified claim: the transcript mentions "Cadence" building scientific research skills, but no such organization was found in the skills ecosystem during source verification.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a coherent architectural vision: the domain expertise gap (the problem) motivates Agent Skills (the solution), which use progressive disclosure and scripts as tools (the mechanisms) to package procedural knowledge in a standardized SKILL.md format (the contract). Skills compose into a converging agent architecture alongside MCP servers (connectivity) and a runtime environment (execution), mapped intuitively via the computing stack analogy. The ecosystem categories demonstrate real adoption, while versioning, testing, and dependency management represent the maturation path. Continuous learning and the collective knowledge base extend skills from individual tools to organizational assets. The open standard ensures portability. Together, these concepts argue that the highest-leverage activity in AI engineering is building composable skills for general-purpose agents rather than rebuilding domain-specific agents — the talk's central thesis.
temporalContext: This talk was presented on December 8, 2025 at the AI Engineering Code Summit, approximately 7 weeks after Anthropic launched Agent Skills on October 16, 2025. The talk references 'five weeks ago' since launch, consistent with the October announcement. Between the talk and the research date (August 21, 2026), significant developments occurred: Anthropic published the Agent Skills open standard (Dec 16, 2025), launched organization-wide skill management and a partner directory (Dec 18, 2025), published the skills-MCP complementarity article (Dec 19, 2025), and released the 'Building Agents with Skills' article (Jan 22, 2026). The talk's future directions — testing, versioning, dependency management, and the open standard — were partially realized within weeks of the presentation, making this talk a snapshot of a rapidly evolving ecosystem at its inflection point.
takeaways: Code is the universal interface to the digital world, making the underlying agent more universal than originally thought
Skills are organized folders of files that package composable procedural knowledge, deliberately simple so anyone can create them
Progressive disclosure shows only metadata at runtime, protecting the context window and enabling hundreds of composable skills
Thousands of skills have been created since launch five weeks ago, spanning foundational, third-party, and enterprise categories
Skills complement MCP servers: MCP provides external connectivity while skills provide domain expertise
Anthropic is moving toward treating skills like software—with testing, evaluation, versioning, and explicit dependency management
Skills enable continuous learning: the standardized format guarantees Claude's written knowledge is efficiently reusable by future versions of itself
The computing analogy: models are processors, agent runtime is the OS, and skills are applications where domain expertise lives

concepts.name: Agent Skills
concepts.explanation: Anthropic's system for packaging composable procedural knowledge as organized folders of files (SKILL.md plus optional scripts and resources) that agents load at runtime to gain domain expertise. Skills are deliberately simple so anyone — human or agent — can create and use them.
concepts.importance: The central concept of the talk and the proposed solution to the domain expertise gap in AI agents. It represents a paradigm shift from building specialized agents to building reusable, composable knowledge packages.

concepts.name: Domain expertise gap in agents
concepts.explanation: The observation that AI agents possess intelligence and general capabilities but lack the domain-specific expertise needed for real-world work, analogous to hiring an experienced tax professional over a mathematical genius for consistent contextual execution.
concepts.importance: Defines the core problem the talk addresses and motivates the entire skills architecture — without this gap, skills would be unnecessary.

concepts.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
concepts.explanation: A protocol created by Anthropic (lead author Mahesh Murag) that provides external connectivity for agents — connecting to APIs, databases, and external services. The talk establishes that MCP and skills are complementary: MCP for connectivity, skills for expertise.
concepts.importance: Defines the connectivity layer of the converging agent architecture and clarifies the boundary between what MCP does (connect) and what skills do (provide expertise), resolving potential architectural overlap.

concepts.name: Converging agent architecture
concepts.explanation: The emerging standard architecture combining four components: an agent loop for context management, a runtime environment with file system and code execution, MCP servers for external connectivity, and a library of skills loaded at runtime. Equipping an agent for a new domain means giving it the right MCP servers and skills.
concepts.importance: Provides the architectural framework that positions skills within the broader agent system, making the talk's recommendations actionable for practitioners.

concepts.name: Continuous learning via skills
concepts.explanation: The capability enabled by the standardized skill format where anything Claude writes as a skill can be used efficiently by a future version of itself, making learning transferable across sessions and model versions. This makes agent memory tangible and persistent.
concepts.importance: Addresses the fundamental limitation that agents do not learn over time, proposing skills as the mechanism for accumulating and transferring knowledge.

concepts.name: Computing stack analogy (models as processors, runtime as OS, skills as applications)
concepts.explanation: The analogy mapping the agent ecosystem to a computing stack: models are like processors (raw compute), agent runtime is like an operating system (resource management and scheduling), and skills are like applications (domain expertise encoded for end users).
concepts.importance: Provides an intuitive mental model for understanding the agent architecture and the strategic positioning of skills, making the talk accessible to a broad audience.

concepts.name: General-purpose agent universality
concepts.explanation: The finding that Claude Code proved to be a general-purpose agent whose scaffolding can be as thin as bash and a file system, demonstrating that the underlying agent is more universal than originally expected and that code is the universal interface.
concepts.importance: Justifies the strategic pivot from building domain-specific agents to building skills for general-purpose agents, which is the talk's central recommendation.

concepts.name: Collective organizational knowledge base
concepts.explanation: The vision of skills as a shared, evolving knowledge base curated by people and agents within organizations, where new team members inherit institutional knowledge and skills compound in value across the organization.
concepts.importance: Frames skills not just as individual tools but as an organizational asset for knowledge management and institutional memory, extending the value proposition beyond individual productivity.

concepts.name: Skill ecosystem categories (foundational, third-party, enterprise)
concepts.explanation: Three categories of skills that emerged since launch: foundational (built by Anthropic, e.g., document skills), third-party (built by partners like Browserbase and Notion), and enterprise (built by Fortune 100 companies and large developer productivity teams).
concepts.importance: Demonstrates real-world adoption and ecosystem maturity, providing evidence that the skills paradigm is scaling beyond theory into practice across multiple sectors.

concepts.name: Agent skills as open standard
concepts.explanation: Agent Skills was published as an open standard (agentskills.io, Apache 2.0 licensed) originally developed by Anthropic, enabling cross-platform portability and community-driven evolution of the specification.
concepts.importance: Ensures skills are not locked to a single vendor or platform, enabling broad ecosystem participation and long-term sustainability of the skills paradigm.

concepts.name: Context window protection via metadata-only loading
concepts.explanation: The practice of showing only skill metadata (name and description) in the system prompt at startup rather than full skill contents, preventing context window exhaustion when hundreds of skills are available. Full content is loaded on-demand only when a skill is invoked.
concepts.importance: The engineering constraint that makes large-scale skill composition practical — without it, adding skills would degrade agent performance by consuming context budget.

concepts.name: Build skills not agents (strategic thesis)
concepts.explanation: The core strategic recommendation that practitioners should stop building domain-specific agents from scratch and instead build reusable, composable skills that equip general-purpose agents with domain expertise.
concepts.importance: The actionable takeaway of the talk that directs engineering effort toward the highest-leverage activity in the agent ecosystem.

concepts.name: Progressive disclosure
concepts.explanation: A context-management pattern where only skill metadata (name and description in YAML frontmatter) is shown to the model at startup; the full SKILL.md body and bundled files are loaded only when the agent decides to use that skill. This three-level approach protects the context window from bloat.
concepts.importance: Core architectural mechanism that makes hundreds of composable skills feasible by preventing context window exhaustion — the primary engineering constraint the talk addresses.

concepts.name: Composable skills as modular packages
concepts.explanation: Skills are self-contained folders of files (SKILL.md plus optional reference files, scripts, and assets) that can be composed together at runtime, analogous to how software modules or packages compose.
concepts.importance: Defines the unit of reuse and composition in the agent architecture, enabling ecosystem growth where independent parties build interoperable capabilities.

concepts.name: Scripts as tools
concepts.explanation: Skills can bundle executable scripts (e.g., Python) that the agent invokes as deterministic tools, solving the problem of traditional tools with ambiguous natural-language instructions that must permanently live in the context window.
concepts.importance: Bridges procedural knowledge packaging with code execution, allowing precise, reusable operations without context bloat.

concepts.name: SKILL.md file format with YAML frontmatter
concepts.explanation: The standardized file at the root of every skill directory, containing YAML frontmatter (name, description metadata) and a Markdown body with instructions. This format is the contract between skill authors and the agent runtime.
concepts.importance: Defines the interface specification that makes skills portable, discoverable, and interoperable across platforms — the foundation of the open standard.

concepts.name: Versioning and lineage for skills
concepts.explanation: The proposed practice of treating skills like software artifacts with version numbers and clear lineage, enabling reproducibility and controlled updates across skill ecosystems.
concepts.importance: Part of the future direction for maturing skills from ad-hoc files to managed software components with predictable upgrade paths.

concepts.name: Explicit dependency management
concepts.explanation: The proposed capability for skills to declare explicit dependencies on other skills, MCP servers, and packages, mirroring dependency management in traditional software ecosystems like npm or pip.
concepts.importance: Enables reliable composition of complex skill stacks and prevents runtime failures from missing prerequisites — essential for enterprise adoption.

concepts.name: Testing and evaluation of skills
concepts.explanation: The proposed practice of applying software testing and evaluation methodologies to skills, ensuring that skills produce predictable, correct outputs before deployment.
concepts.importance: Critical for enterprise trust and for scaling skills from hundreds to thousands without quality degradation.

concepts.name: Git-based skill distribution
concepts.explanation: Skills work with existing infrastructure like Git repositories and Google Drive, meaning standard version control and file-sharing systems serve as the distribution mechanism without requiring bespoke platforms.
concepts.importance: Lowers the barrier to adoption by leveraging ubiquitous developer tooling rather than requiring new infrastructure.

concepts.name: Code as universal interface
concepts.explanation: The thesis that code is not just a use case for agents but the universal interface to the digital world, meaning a general-purpose agent with code execution capabilities can interact with any digital system.
concepts.importance: Foundational engineering principle justifying the shift from domain-specific agents to general-purpose agents equipped with skills.

concepts.name: Agent runtime environment
concepts.explanation: The execution environment providing a file system, code execution capability, and the agent loop — analogous to an operating system that manages resources and schedules work for the model (processor).
concepts.importance: Defines the platform layer on which skills are loaded and executed, making the computing stack analogy concrete and implementable.

concepts.name: Skill creator skill (meta-tooling)
concepts.explanation: A skill that enables Claude to create new skills autonomously, serving as meta-tooling for automated skill generation and a foundation for continuous learning loops.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that skill creation is itself composable, enabling scalable ecosystem growth where agents contribute skills back to the knowledge base.

sections.title: Introduction and the expertise gap
sections.summary: Barry and Mahesh introduce the talk, noting agents now have intelligence but lack domain expertise. They describe how the ecosystem matured with MCP, Claude Code, and the agent SDK, and present their thesis that code is the universal interface and agents are more universal than expected.

sections.title: What skills are and how they work
sections.summary: Skills are introduced as organized folders of files packaging procedural knowledge. They can include scripts as tools, use progressive disclosure to protect context windows, and work with existing infrastructure like Git and Google Drive.

sections.title: The skills ecosystem and categories
sections.summary: Since launch five weeks ago, thousands of skills have emerged in three categories: foundational (Anthropic document skills, Cadence research skills), third-party (Browserbase, Notion), and enterprise (Fortune 100 companies, developer productivity teams).

sections.title: Observed trends in the skills ecosystem
sections.summary: Three trends are observed: skills are becoming more complex (packaging binaries, executables, assets), skills are complementing MCP servers by orchestrating multi-tool workflows, and non-technical users in finance, legal, recruiting, and accounting are building skills.

sections.title: The emerging agent architecture
sections.summary: The converging agent architecture combines an agent loop for context management, a runtime environment with file system and code execution, MCP servers for external connectivity, and a library of skills loaded at runtime. Equipping an agent for a new domain now means giving it the right MCP servers and skills.

sections.title: Future directions: treating skills like software
sections.summary: Anthropic launched financial services and life sciences offerings with bundled MCP servers and skills. Future directions include testing and evaluation, versioning with clear lineage, and explicit dependencies on other skills, MCP servers, and packages to improve predictability and composability.

sections.title: Sharing, distribution, and continuous learning
sections.summary: The vision is a collective, evolving knowledge base curated by people and agents within organizations. New team members inherit institutional knowledge. Skills make memory tangible and enable continuous learning—anything Claude writes can be reused efficiently by future versions of itself. Claude can already create skills via the skill creator skill.

sections.title: Computing analogy and conclusion
sections.summary: The closing analogy compares models to processors, agent runtime to operating systems, and skills to applications where domain expertise lives. The call to action: stop rebuilding agents, start building skills. Anthropic invites collaboration.

organization.name: Anthropic
organization.summary: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company that builds reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems. It is a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation headquartered in San Francisco whose purpose is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. Anthropic created Agent Skills, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Claude Code, and the Claude Agent SDK — all referenced in this talk as part of the converging agent architecture. The company employs both speakers Barry Zhang and Mahesh Murag, who co-created the Agent Skills system. Anthropic's products include Claude, Claude Code, Skills, and Claude Science, with a board including Dario Amodei (CEO) and Daniela Amodei (President).

technologies.label: Agent Skills
technologies.summary: Agent Skills is Anthropic's system for packaging composable procedural knowledge as organized folders of files. Each skill contains a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter metadata and Markdown instructions, optionally bundling scripts and reference files. Progressive disclosure shows only metadata at runtime to protect context windows, enabling hundreds of composable skills. Scripts within skills serve as deterministic tools, solving limitations of traditional tools with ambiguous instructions. Since the October 2025 launch, thousands of skills have been created across foundational (Anthropic document skills), third-party (Browserbase, Notion), and enterprise (Fortune 100 companies) categories. Skills work with existing infrastructure like Git and Google Drive. Claude can autonomously create skills via the skill creator skill, enabling continuous learning loops where knowledge is transferable across sessions and model versions.
technologies.role: Primary technology presented as the solution to the domain expertise gap. The talk's core thesis is 'stop building agents, build skills instead.' Skills are positioned as applications in the computing stack analogy where models are processors and runtime is the OS.

technologies.label: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
technologies.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a protocol created by Anthropic (lead author Mahesh Murag, co-presenter of this talk) that provides external connectivity for agents, connecting them to APIs, databases, and external services. In the talk's architecture, MCP and Agent Skills are explicitly complementary: MCP provides the connection to the outside world while skills provide domain expertise. MCP became the connectivity standard in the agent ecosystem. The talk notes that equipping an agent for a new domain now means giving it the right MCP servers and skills. Anthropic also bundled MCP servers with skills in their financial services and life sciences offerings.
technologies.role: Complementary technology providing the external connectivity layer of the converging agent architecture. Positioned alongside skills as one of the two key components for equipping agents for real-world work.

technologies.label: Claude Code and Agent Runtime
technologies.summary: Claude Code is Anthropic's general-purpose agent product that proved the thesis that code is the universal interface to the digital world and that the underlying agent is more universal than originally expected. Claude Code demonstrated that agent scaffolding can be as thin as bash and a file system. It serves as the primary runtime environment where Agent Skills are loaded and executed. The Claude Agent SDK extends this capability for developers building custom agents. Together, they form the runtime layer of the converging agent architecture — analogous to an operating system managing resources for the model (processor) in the talk's computing stack analogy.
technologies.role: General-purpose agent product proving code is the universal interface and agents are more universal than expected. Serves as the runtime environment (OS layer in the computing analogy) where skills (applications) are loaded and executed.

technologies.label: Agent Skills Open Standard
technologies.summary: The Agent Skills Open Standard is the standardized specification for the Agent Skills format, published as an open standard (Apache 2.0 licensed) at agentskills.io on December 16, 2025. Originally developed by Anthropic, it was released as an open standard to enable cross-platform portability and community-driven evolution. The standard realizes the talk's future direction of treating skills like software — with versioning, clear lineage, explicit dependencies on other skills, MCP servers, and packages, and testing and evaluation. Skills work with existing infrastructure like Git repositories, lowering adoption barriers. The standardized format also enables continuous learning: anything Claude writes as a skill can be used efficiently by a future version of itself, making learning transferable across platforms and model versions.
technologies.role: Represents the future direction of skills as a standardized, portable format. The talk foreshadowed standardization as part of treating skills like software with testing, versioning, and explicit dependencies. This was realized as an open standard within weeks of the talk.

outcomes: Explain why domain expertise rather than intelligence alone is needed for agents to perform real-world work, using the tax professional vs mathematical genius analogy
Describe the structure of agent skills as organized folders of files with SKILL.md, YAML frontmatter, and progressive disclosure across three levels
Articulate how progressive disclosure protects context windows by showing only metadata at startup, enabling hundreds of composable skills to coexist
Explain the complementary relationship between skills and MCP servers: MCP provides external connectivity while skills provide domain expertise and procedural knowledge
Identify the three categories of skills (foundational, third-party, enterprise) and provide real-world examples of each including Anthropic document skills, Browserbase, and Notion partner skills
Describe the converging agent architecture combining an agent loop, runtime environment with file system and code execution, MCP servers, and a library of skills loaded at runtime
Apply the computing stack analogy (models as processors, agent runtime as OS, skills as applications) to reason about agent system design
Explain how skills enable continuous learning by guaranteeing that knowledge written by Claude is efficiently reusable by future versions of itself

challengeSeeds: Build your first skill: Create a SKILL.md for a task you perform repeatedly with Claude, using YAML frontmatter with name and description, and at least two levels of progressive disclosure to keep context lean

Multi-file skill design: Take a complex workflow such as financial report generation and decompose it into a SKILL.md plus linked reference files (e.g., reference.md, forms.md), keeping the core lean and loading details only when needed

Script as tool: Write a deterministic Python script that performs a specific operation (e.g., PDF form field extraction, data sorting) and bundle it inside a skill directory as a reusable tool that Claude executes without loading into context

Skills plus MCP integration: Design an agent architecture that pairs an MCP server for external connectivity with a skill for domain expertise, and explain how the skill orchestrates multi-tool workflows across the MCP connection

Skill ecosystem audit: Select an existing skill from anthropics/skills or a partner repository (e.g., browserbase/skills) and evaluate it for progressive disclosure effectiveness, security considerations, and composability with other skills

Continuous learning skill: Design a skill that captures an agent's successful approaches and common mistakes from a completed task so that future versions of the agent can reuse that knowledge efficiently
